summary: On a mission to Mars, a message to a doctor on Earth takes up to 22 minutes each way, and there is no evacuation. Astronauts must notice health problems, judge how serious they are and act, largely on their own. VoidHealth is an offline health monitor that astronauts run themselves. A guided daily check-in explains how to take each measurement in space and why it matters. An interactive body map shows nine body systems, each tied to NASA's five hazards of human spaceflight and the matching Human Research Program risk. Readings are color-coded against normal ranges and the astronaut's own pre-flight baseline, and combined rules catch conditions such as Spaceflight Associated Neuro-ocular Syndrome. Every finding is assigned to whoever should act (the astronaut, the crew medical officer, or the flight surgeon on Earth) with step-by-step protocols and a ground report written for the communication delay. Built-in exams include a reaction test, an Amsler vision grid, a mood check-in and a camera-based pulse measurement. It runs on the web and as desktop software, fully offline.
details:
Guided daily check-in: step-by-step instructions for blood pressure, heart rate, blood oxygen, temperature, glucose, sleep, body mass, hydration and exercise, adapted for microgravity (for example, body mass uses an oscillation device, since scales do not work without gravity).

Interactive body map: nine clickable body systems (brain, eyes, heart, lungs, immune system, metabolism, kidneys, bones, muscles). Each shows its function, how spaceflight affects it, the NASA HRP risk it maps to, the astronaut's readings, countermeasures, and when to escalate.

In-app exams: a 3-minute reaction test based on the PVT-B used in spaceflight research; an Amsler grid for vision distortion linked to SANS; a mood and stress check-in for isolation effects; and a camera pulse measurement using remote photoplethysmography.

Assessment and triage: readings are compared with normal ranges and the astronaut's personal pre-flight baseline. Rules combine signals (a distorted Amsler grid plus blurred vision plus raised blood pressure means possible SANS), and every finding is routed to self-care, the crew medical officer or the flight surgeon.

Protocols and ground report: offline checklists for solar particle events, vision changes, fever, CO2 build-up, fatigue, dizziness after landing and more. The ground report packages the data for Earth and shows the real one-way signal delay.

Mission environments: low Earth orbit, lunar surface, Mars transit and Mars surface. Each changes gravity, radiation dose rate, exercise targets and signal delay, using measured dose rates (Curiosity RAD, Chang'e 4 LND).

Radiation and bone tracking: cumulative dose against NASA's 600 mSv career limit, and a bone mineral loss estimate based on gravity and exercise.

Trends: charts against normal range and personal baseline, plus on-device trend detection, projections and correlations.

Simulate anomaly: inject a solar storm, vision change, fatigue, infection, CO2 build-up or post-landing dizziness to see how detection and guidance respond.

Routine and motivation: daily schedule, streaks, ranks and mission patches to keep the routine going across months.

Benefits and impact

It reduces dependence on Earth for routine health decisions, catches slow changes early by comparing each astronaut with themselves, and makes sure the right person acts. Because it runs offline on common devices and explains everything in plain language, the same approach could serve Antarctic stations, ships, rural clinics and disaster zones on Earth.

How we built it

TypeScript, React, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Zustand, Recharts and Motion for the interface; Electron for the Windows and Linux desktop apps; FFmpeg for the demo video. All data stays on the device; there is no server. Crew history in the demo is simulated using published effect sizes and dose rates, and anything entered or measured in the app is real and evaluated the same way.

What makes it creative

Triage designed around communication delay, personal baselines instead of Earth-only norms, rules that combine symptoms the way a clinician would, exams that need nothing but a screen and a camera, and a ground report written to be read cold, hours later.

Factors we considered

No internet in deep space, astronauts who are not doctors, months-long missions, privacy of medical data, and clear limits: VoidHealth is decision support, not a medical device.
